title: From Bean to Cup
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Coffee is one of the most widely traded products in the world, and billions of cups are drunk every day. According to a popular legend, its effect was first noticed in Ethiopia by a goatherd named Kaldi, who saw that his goats became lively after eating the red berries of a certain bush. Whatever the truth of the tale, coffee drinking was well established in the Arab world by the fifteenth century, and the port of Mocha in Yemen gave its name to a famous type of coffee, which is still sold under that name today.

Coffee grows on evergreen bushes, mostly in a belt around the equator, at heights between six hundred and two thousand metres. The two main species are Arabica, which has a fine flavour and makes up about sixty per cent of the world's coffee, and Robusta, which is stronger, more bitter and easier to grow. A bush begins to bear fruit after about three years. The fruits, called cherries, turn from green to bright red when they are ripe, and a single bush produces enough cherries for about half a kilogram of roasted coffee each year.

On many farms the harvest is carried out by hand, since the cherries on a bush ripen at different times and must be picked one by one. A good worker can pick between one hundred and two hundred kilograms of cherries in a day. On large, flat plantations, as in Brazil, machines shake the bushes and collect everything at once, which is faster but lowers quality because unripe cherries are included. The choice of method depends on the shape of the land and on the price that the farmer expects to receive.

After picking, the seeds, which are called beans, must be removed from the fruit. This stage is known as processing, and there are two main methods. In the dry method, the cherries are spread out in the sun for several weeks and turned regularly, and then the dried skin is broken off. In the wet method, the fruit is washed away with water in a machine, and the beans are left to ferment for a day before they are dried. The wet method produces a cleaner and brighter flavour but uses large amounts of water, which can pollute rivers if it is not treated.

Roasting turns the pale green beans brown and creates the flavour. During roasting, which takes between ten and twenty minutes, the beans reach a temperature of more than two hundred degrees Celsius, and they pop with a sound like popcorn and double in size. A light roast keeps more of the original taste of the bean, while a dark roast has a strong, smoky flavour. Once the beans are roasted they begin to lose their freshness, so many coffee lovers buy whole beans and grind them just before making a drink.

The final stage is brewing, in which hot water takes the flavour out of ground coffee. There are many methods. An espresso machine forces hot water through finely ground coffee at high pressure, and makes a small, strong cup; filter coffee is made by letting the water drip slowly through a paper filter; and in Turkey and parts of Central Asia, coffee is boiled with the grounds in a small pot with a long handle. The grounds sink to the bottom of the cup, and the drinker must leave the last mouthful.

Behind the pleasure of a cup of coffee lie serious problems. Most farmers are poor, and receive only a small share of the price that the customer pays in a cafe. Climate change is making some areas too warm for Arabica, and scientists warn that a large part of the land now used for it may become unsuitable within decades. Some companies have therefore begun to pay farmers higher prices for coffee grown in ways that protect the forest, a practice known as fair trade, though critics say that its benefits are limited.
